title: Digital Assets for Boards
summary: A ten-module programme giving boards and directors the understanding and tools to oversee digital asset activities and evidence sound oversight to regulators.
intro: This training programme equips boards and directors to oversee digital asset activities with confidence: understanding the products, challenging strategy, setting risk appetite and evidencing sound oversight to regulators.

sections.Aim and Purpose: To give directors a practical, jargon-free grounding in crypto-assets, stablecoins and tokenisation, the business models built on them and the risks they bring. Participants leave able to challenge management's digital asset strategy, set clear risk appetite and evidence effective oversight to supervisors and auditors.
sections.What It Covers: Crypto-assets, stablecoins and tokenisation, strategic opportunity and business model risk, custody and safeguarding, financial crime, market integrity, technology and cyber risk, international regulatory approaches, risk appetite, board oversight questions and a board action plan.
Intended Audience: Chairs, non-executive and independent directors of firms offering, or planning to offer, digital asset products and services
Executive directors and senior managers accountable for digital asset strategy, risk, compliance and operations
Board committee members and company secretaries supporting oversight of new business lines
Learning Objectives: Explain in plain language how crypto-assets, stablecoins and tokenised assets work and where the firm is exposed to them
Challenge management's digital asset strategy, business case and business model assumptions
Assess custody, safeguarding, financial crime and market integrity risks using structured board-level questions
Evaluate technology, cyber and third-party risk in digital asset operations
Compare international regulatory approaches and what supervisors expect of boards
Set a digital asset risk appetite and agree a board action plan
sections.Structure and Format: Ten modules of about two hours each, delivered in person, virtually or in a hybrid format, either as a two- to three-day programme or as a series of board briefing sessions. Each module combines a short briefing with case studies and a board question set, and modules can be selected or tailored to the board's needs.
sections.Useful Prior Knowledge and Experience: Board or senior management experience in financial services is helpful. No technical background in blockchain or digital assets is required.
Core Reading: FSB, High-level Recommendations for the Regulation, Supervision and Oversight of Crypto-Asset Activities and Markets (2023)
IOSCO, Policy Recommendations for Crypto and Digital Asset Markets (2023)
Basel Committee, Prudential Treatment of Cryptoasset Exposures (2022)

modules.title: Digital Assets for Directors
modules.summary: Plain-language grounding in distributed ledgers, crypto-assets, stablecoins and tokenised assets, how they differ from traditional instruments and why they change the firm's risk profile.
objectives: Explain how blockchains, tokens and digital wallets work
Distinguish crypto-assets, stablecoins, tokenised securities and central bank digital currencies
Identify where the firm is already exposed to digital assets, directly or through clients and partners
syllabus: Distributed ledgers, consensus and smart contracts in plain language
Types of digital asset and how each is used
Stablecoins: reserve models, redemption and run risk
The vocabulary directors need: keys, wallets, staking, DeFi, on-chain and off-chain

modules.title: Strategy, Opportunity and Business Model Risk
modules.summary: How boards test whether digital assets fit the firm's strategy, challenge management's business case and recognise the business model risks that have caused failures in the sector.
objectives: Challenge the strategic rationale and claimed benefits of a digital asset proposition
Assess revenue concentration, volatility and dependency in digital asset business models
Recognise the business model weaknesses behind high-profile sector failures
syllabus: Business models: trading, custody, issuance, payments, tokenisation and infrastructure
Questions to ask of a business case: demand, cost, capability, dependency and exit
Conflicts of interest in vertically integrated platforms
Case studies of sector failures and the governance lessons

modules.title: Custody, Safeguarding and Client Assets
modules.summary: Why custody is the critical risk in digital assets, how client assets are held and protected, and what assurance the board needs that client holdings are safe and reconciled.
objectives: Explain how private keys, wallets and custody arrangements protect or expose client assets
Evaluate segregation, reconciliation and safeguarding controls
Judge the adequacy of independent assurance over client holdings
syllabus: Hot, warm and cold storage, multi-signature and key management
Segregation of client assets and treatment on insolvency
Reconciliation, proof of reserves and their limits
Sub-custody and third-party custodian due diligence

modules.title: Financial Crime and Sanctions Risk
modules.summary: The money laundering, terrorist financing, sanctions and fraud risks specific to digital assets, and the controls and management information the board should expect.
objectives: Explain the main financial crime typologies involving digital assets
Assess the firm's financial crime risk assessment, controls and use of analytics
Oversee sanctions exposure and suspicious activity reporting
syllabus: Typologies: mixers, privacy coins, ransomware, scams and nested exchanges
FATF standards for virtual assets and the travel rule
Blockchain analytics, transaction monitoring and their limits
Board-level financial crime MI and escalation

modules.title: Market Integrity and Client Outcomes
modules.summary: How manipulation, conflicts and poor disclosure arise in digital asset markets, and how the board gains assurance that clients are treated fairly and markets operate with integrity.
objectives: Recognise market abuse and manipulation patterns in digital asset markets
Assess conflicts of interest, listing decisions and client disclosures
Evaluate whether products are appropriate for the clients they reach
syllabus: Wash trading, pump-and-dump schemes and insider dealing
Token listing and delisting governance
Financial promotions, marketing and retail client appropriateness
Complaints, client outcomes and redress

modules.title: Technology, Cyber and Third-Party Risk
modules.summary: How digital asset operations fail and are attacked, how dependency on protocols and providers concentrates risk, and whether the firm can withstand and recover from a serious incident.
objectives: Recognise the main technology and cyber threats to digital asset operations
Assess dependency on blockchains, protocols and critical third parties
Evaluate incident response, resilience testing and escalation to the board
syllabus: Hacks, key compromise, smart contract bugs and bridge exploits
Protocol, network and oracle dependency risk
Outsourcing and critical third-party oversight
Incident response and recovery: what the board should require

modules.title: International Regulatory Approaches and Supervisory Expectations
modules.summary: How jurisdictions are regulating crypto-assets and stablecoins, how this overlays existing financial services rules, and what supervisors expect to see from the board.
objectives: Explain the main regulatory approaches to crypto-assets, stablecoins and tokenisation
Identify the licensing, conduct and prudential duties likely to apply to the firm
Prepare the board to evidence oversight to supervisors
syllabus: International standards: FSB, IOSCO, FATF, Basel Committee and CPMI
Regional crypto-asset regimes, stablecoin rules and tokenisation pilots
Prudential treatment of crypto-asset exposures
Operating across jurisdictions: licensing, passporting limits and divergence

modules.title: Risk Appetite for Digital Assets
modules.summary: How boards decide which digital asset activities the firm will and will not undertake, and set a risk appetite with measurable limits, triggers and escalation.
objectives: Set a digital asset risk appetite with clear in-scope and prohibited activities
Define limits and key risk indicators for exposure, counterparties and products
Link risk appetite to capital, liquidity and wind-down planning
syllabus: Drafting a risk appetite statement for digital assets
Limits on exposures, counterparties, assets and client types
Stress scenarios: price collapse, stablecoin de-peg and platform failure
Orderly exit and wind-down planning

modules.title: Board Oversight, Information and Assurance
modules.summary: The information boards need to oversee digital asset activities, how to read reports critically and how to obtain credible independent assurance rather than relying on assertion.
objectives: Specify the management information and indicators the board needs
Interpret digital asset reports and identify what is missing
Obtain assurance from the control functions, internal audit and external reviewers
syllabus: The core board information set: exposures, client assets, incidents and financial crime
Committee mandates and the three lines of defence for digital assets
Recognising comfort without evidence
A board question set for approving, expanding or exiting an activity

modules.title: Leading Digital Asset Oversight: Board Action Plan
modules.summary: Brings the programme together into a board action plan covering the board's own capability, emerging developments such as tokenised markets and decentralised finance, and keeping governance current.
objectives: Assess the board's digital asset literacy and plan to close gaps
Anticipate governance issues from tokenisation, decentralised finance and new market infrastructure
Produce a board action plan for digital asset oversight
syllabus: Board skills, external advice and how much expertise is enough
Tokenised deposits, securities and funds: what comes next
Decentralised finance and accountability questions
Workshop: the board's twelve-month digital asset oversight plan
